title: Modern management and an intro to Microsoft Intune
summary: See how endpoint management moved from on-prem domain joins and imaging to cloud-based management, then tour Microsoft Intune and the admin center you will use every day.
objectives: Contrast traditional management (AD + Group Policy + imaging) with modern cloud management
Describe what Microsoft Intune is and where it fits in Microsoft Intune Suite and Microsoft 365
Navigate the Microsoft Intune admin center and find devices, apps, and policies
Explain the role of the Intune MDM and how a device 'enrolls'
Identify the difference between MDM and MAM at a high level
Know what an Endpoint Administrator does and how MD-102 maps to the job

quiz.q: What is the biggest shift that 'modern management' represents compared with traditional management?
options: Devices are managed from the cloud instead of requiring an on-prem domain and Group Policy
Users can no longer install any apps
Imaging every device by hand becomes mandatory
quiz.why: Modern management uses cloud services like Intune and Entra ID so a device can be configured and secured over the internet, without needing a line of sight to an on-prem domain controller or hand-built images.

quiz.q: Which portal is the primary place an Endpoint Administrator works in day to day?
quiz.why: The Microsoft Intune admin center (intune.microsoft.com) is the unified console for devices, apps, configuration, compliance, and security policies.

quiz.q: What does MDM stand for, and what does it manage?
options: Managed Data Migration — it moves files
Mobile Device Management — it manages the whole device
Memory Defragment Manager — it tunes RAM
quiz.why: MDM (Mobile Device Management) enrolls and manages an entire device: its settings, compliance, apps, and security posture from the cloud.

quiz.q: How does MAM differ from MDM?
options: MAM encrypts the hard drive only
MAM manages company app data without managing the whole device
quiz.why: MAM (Mobile Application Management) protects corporate data inside specific apps (like Outlook) without taking management control of the entire personal device.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is device 'enrollment'?
quiz.answer: Enrollment is the process where a device registers with Intune so it can receive and report on policies, apps, and compliance.
quiz.why: Until a device is enrolled, Intune has no management relationship with it, so it cannot push configuration or read compliance state.

quiz.q: Name one real benefit of cloud management for a remote or hybrid workforce.
quiz.answer: Devices can be configured, secured, and supported over the internet without needing to be on the corporate network or VPN.
quiz.why: Cloud management removes the on-prem line-of-sight requirement, which is essential when staff work from anywhere.

Microsoft — Exam MD-102: Microsoft 365 Endpoint Administrator

body_markdown:
## From the old world to the cloud

If you have worked Tier 1, you have probably met **traditional management**: a Windows PC joined to an on-premises **Active Directory** domain, pushed settings via **Group Policy**, and built from a hand-crafted **image**. It works, but it assumes the device is on the corporate network and that someone built that image by hand.

**Modern management** flips this. The device is managed from the **cloud**, over the internet, from anywhere. Settings, apps, and security all flow down from a cloud service. This matters enormously for a hybrid and remote workforce — the PC at someone's kitchen table is just as manageable as the one in the office.

## What is Microsoft Intune?

**Microsoft Intune** is Microsoft's cloud service for managing devices and apps. It is the engine of modern management. Intune can manage Windows, macOS, iOS/iPadOS, and Android, and it sits inside the broader **Microsoft 365** and **Microsoft Intune Suite** family alongside Entra ID and Defender.

Intune does the jobs you used to do by hand or with Group Policy: deploy apps, push **configuration profiles**, enforce **compliance**, and apply security baselines — all from one console.

## MDM vs MAM

Two terms you will hear constantly:

- **MDM (Mobile Device Management)** manages the *whole device*. Think company-owned laptops fully enrolled into Intune.
- **MAM (Mobile Application Management)** protects company *data inside apps* without managing the whole device. Think a personal phone where only the Outlook work account is protected.

Knowing which one applies tells you how much control you have and what you can troubleshoot.

## A tour of the admin center

The console you will live in is the **Microsoft Intune admin center**.

```text
1. Go to https://intune.microsoft.com
2. Sign in with an admin account
3. Left menu, explore the key blades:
   - Devices  -> enrolled devices and their state
   - Apps     -> what you deploy to devices
   - Endpoint security -> baselines, antivirus, Defender
   - Reports  -> compliance and deployment status
   - Tenant administration -> connectors and roles
```

Spend time here. Click **Devices**, pick one, and look at its hardware, compliance, and the policies applied to it. This single device blade answers most Tier 2 questions.

## Enrollment in one sentence

**Enrollment** is the moment a device registers with Intune so it can receive policies and report back. No enrollment, no management relationship — so when a policy 'isn't applying', the first question is often: *is the device actually enrolled and checking in?*

## The role and the exam

The job title is **Endpoint Administrator**, and the certification that maps to it is **MD-102**. As you move from Tier 1 to Tier 2, you stop just resetting passwords and start owning device configuration, app delivery, and compliance. This month builds exactly those skills.

## Your task

Sign in to the Microsoft Intune admin center, open the **Devices** blade, pick any enrolled device, and write down three facts about it: its compliance state, its operating system version, and one policy applied to it.

slides.narration: Welcome to Month Five. This is where you step up from Tier One into real endpoint administration. Today we'll see how device management moved from the old on-prem world into the cloud, and then we'll meet Microsoft Intune, the tool you'll be using every single day from here on. By the end you'll know what Intune is, where it fits, and how to find your way around the admin center.

slides.title: The old world
bullets: PCs joined to an on-prem Active Directory domain.
Settings pushed by Group Policy.
Machines built from hand-made images.
Assumes the device is on the corporate network.
slides.narration: Let's start with what you probably already know. Traditional management means a Windows PC joined to an on-premises Active Directory domain. Settings come down through Group Policy, and the machine was built from an image someone crafted by hand. It works, but it quietly assumes the device is sitting on the corporate network. That assumption breaks the moment people work from home.

slides.title: Modern management
bullets: Devices managed from the cloud, over the internet.
No line of sight to a domain controller needed.
The kitchen-table laptop is as manageable as the office one.
Built for a hybrid, remote workforce.
slides.narration: Modern management flips all of that. Instead of relying on the corporate network, the device is managed from the cloud, over the internet, from anywhere on earth. Settings, apps, and security all flow down from a cloud service. That means the laptop at someone's kitchen table is just as manageable as the one in the office. This is the world MD-102 is built around.

slides.title: What is Intune?
bullets: Microsoft's cloud service for managing devices and apps.
Manages Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android.
Lives inside Microsoft 365 and the Intune Suite.
Replaces hand-work and much of Group Policy.
slides.narration: Microsoft Intune is the engine of modern management. It's Microsoft's cloud service for managing both devices and apps, and it handles Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android. It sits inside the wider Microsoft 365 family, right next to Entra ID and Defender. The jobs you used to do by hand, or with Group Policy, Intune now does from one console in the cloud.

slides.title: MDM versus MAM

MAM protects company data inside apps only.
MDM: company-owned, fully enrolled laptops.
MAM: a personal phone with just the work account protected.

M A M, Mobile Application Management, protects only company data inside specific apps, without managing the whole device, think a personal phone where only the work email is locked down. Knowing which one applies tells you how much control you actually have.

Devices blade: enrolled devices and their state.
Apps, Endpoint security, Reports.
One device's page answers most Tier 2 questions.

slides.narration: The console you'll live in is the Microsoft Intune admin center, at intune dot microsoft dot com. On the left you'll find the key sections: Devices, where every enrolled device lives; Apps, what you deploy; Endpoint security, for baselines and Defender; and Reports. Honestly, one device's own page, showing its hardware, compliance, and applied policies, answers most of the Tier Two questions you'll get.

slides.title: What is enrollment?
bullets: The moment a device registers with Intune.
Lets the device receive policies and report back.
No enrollment means no management relationship.
'Policy not applying?' Check it's enrolled and checking in.
slides.narration: Enrollment is the moment a device registers with Intune so it can receive policies and report its state back. This is fundamental: without enrollment, there's simply no management relationship, and Intune can't push anything. So when someone says a policy isn't applying, your very first question is often, is this device actually enrolled and checking in? You'd be surprised how often that's the whole answer.
